preamble.summary: Short, fierce, and focused on the fall of Nineveh. LXX Nahum tracks MT closely. Its one direct NT citation is at Romans 10:15, where Paul quotes Nahum 1:15 (LXX 2:1) — 'how beautiful are the feet of those who preach good news' — in its LXX form as his scriptural warrant for Gentile missionary preaching.
preamble.notable_variants: The versification offset (Nahum 1:15 MT = 2:1 LXX); the LXX's rendering of the good-news-messenger vocabulary that Paul inherits for gospel-preaching; the divine-attributes clauses in ch 1 that echo Exodus 34:6 and Joel 2:13.
preamble.theological_legacy: Nahum 1:15 in its LXX form is one of the classic NT proof-texts for the legitimacy of the itinerant Christian missionary. The image of feet-on-mountains-bearing-good-news — shared with Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15 — supplied the whole word-field from which evangelism theology is built.

renderings.mt_reading: הִנֵּה עַל־הֶהָרִים רַגְלֵי מְבַשֵּׂר מַשְׁמִיעַ שָׁלוֹם
renderings.lxx_reading: ἰδοὺ ἐπὶ τὰ ὄρη οἱ πόδες εὐαγγελιζομένου καὶ ἀπαγγέλλοντος εἰρήνην
renderings.mt_rendering: On the mountains — the feet of one who brings good news, who announces peace
renderings.lxx_rendering: Behold on the mountains the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace
notes: Romans 10:15 ('how beautiful are the feet of those who preach good news') quotes this verse in a composite form that fuses LXX Nahum 1:15 with LXX Isaiah 52:7. Both LXX texts use the same euangelizomenou vocabulary — the verb behind the NT noun euangelion ('gospel').

The LXX's euangelizomenou at Nahum 1:15 and Isaiah 52:7 is the single most consequential OT verb for NT theology: the one who 'announces good news.' The noun euangelion and the whole NT gospel-vocabulary descend from this LXX root.

Hebrew mebasser ('one who announces good tidings') is the direct equivalent of Greek euangelizomenos. The LXX established the verbal equivalence that made possible the Christian technical use of euangelion.
